Semantic Analysis

Syntax Analysis: Parser
• The parser receives the tokens from the lexical analyzer and checks if they arrive in the correct order
• It involves grouping the tokens into grammatical phrases that are used by the compiler to produce output. 
• In general, the syntax of a programming language is described by a context-free grammar. 
• The job of the parser is to recover the hierarchical structure of the program from the stream of tokens received 
from the lexical analyzer. 
• The implementation of the compiler depends on the output of the parser: usually a tree 
• Parse tree: describes the syntactical structure of the input 
• Syntax tree: a compressed representation of the parse tree in which the operators appear as the interior node 
and the operands of an operator are the children of the node
3

What is Syntactic Analysis?
• int a;
• a = "hello";                                                                   // Error: assigning string to int
• Syntax analysis: Says “grammar is fine”(The assignment statement has a valid syntactic structure)
• Semantic analysis: Says “type mismatch: int variable cannot hold a string”.
4
Other semantic checks such as:
•
Type checking → Example: You can’t add an integer to a string unless the language defines how 
to do that.
•
Variable declarations → Every variable must be declared before it is used.
•
Scope rules → A variable can only be used in the scope it’s visible in.
•
Function usage → The number and types of arguments must match the function definition.
•
Control flow rules → Statements like break must be inside loops, return must be inside functions.
Syntax asks “Is the structure correct?”  while semantics asks “Does it make sense?”

Contd.,
5
1. Variable declaration check: (1) Is b declared before the if (b == 0)?, 
(2) Is a declared before use?
2. Type Checking: (1) b == 0 → Both sides should be comparable (ex: 
int with int),  (2) a != 1 → must be comparable types, (3) a = b; → If a 
and b have different types (int vs. string) → type mismatch error. (4) a 
= a - 1; → The - operator must be valid for the type (numeric).
3. Function and Member Access Checks : stdio.print(a)
1. stdio must be a valid identifier in scope (library/module).
2. print must be a valid member/function of stdio.
3. Arguments passed (a) must match the expected type of print.
4. Control Flow Rules: (1) if_stmt → 
Condition must be a Boolean expression 
(result of b == 0 must be Boolean). (2) 
while_stmt → Condition must also be 
Boolean (a != 1).
5. Scope Checking: Here, a is used in both the if 
and while — so a must be in the required scope.

Parsing
• Parsing: recognizing whether a program (or sentence) is grammatically well formed, according to the 
rules of a language.
• Main purpose: It identifies the role/function of each component in the input.
6
Compiler connection: In compiler design, the parser performs the same task for programming-language 
tokens, checking whether they follow the grammar.

Parsing Trees
• A parse tree pictorially shows: How the start symbol of a grammar derives strings in language.
7
1. The root is labelled by start symbol 
2. Each leaf is labelled by a terminal (T) or by ϵ 
3. Each interior node is labelled by a non-terminals (NT) 
4. Production rule: If A has children X, Y, Z, then the grammar contains a production such as A → XYZ. 
5. Left-to-right order: Children are arranged from left to right according to their order in the production. 
6. Epsilon production: If a production derives ε, the corresponding node may have ε as its single child.

Parsing Trees: Properties
• A tree consists of one or more nodes 
• Exactly one root node in a Tree
 
– Root has no parent, it is the top node
 
– Other nodes have exactly one parent 
• Leaf: node with no children 
• N is the parent of M, M is the child of N, Children of one node are siblings, 
Ordered from left to right 
• Descendent (self, child*), Ancestor (self, parent*)
8

Contd.,
• Input: stream of tokens 
• Output: abstract syntax tree 
 
– Abstract syntax tree removes extra syntax 
 
 
 
a + b ≈ (a) + (b) ≈ ((a)+((b))) 
9
Note: The parser converts the token stream into a structured representation 
that later compiler phases can process easily.

The Functionality of the Parser 
• Input: sequence of tokens from lexer.
• Output: parse tree of the program.
10

What Parsing doesn’t do 
• Doesn’t check many things: type agreement, variables declared, variables initialized, etc.
 
 Postponed until semantic analysis 
11
Parsing ≠ Full Program Correctness
•
The parser’s job is only to check whether the program’s structure matches the grammar rules 
— the "shape" of the code.
•
It does not:
•
Check if types match (type agreement).
•
Verify if variables are declared before use.
•
Ensure variables are initialized before being read.

Outline
• Regular languages revisited
• Parser overview
• Context-free grammars (CFG’s)
• Derivations
• Ambiguity
• Syntax errors 
12
The flow: Regular Languages → Parser → CFG → Derivations → Ambiguity → Syntax Errors

Languages and Automata 
• Formal languages are very important in CS
• Especially in programming languages
• Formal languages provide mathematical rules for describing valid strings.
• Regular languages
• The weakest formal languages widely used (regular expressions and finite automata)
• Many applications (can recognize identifiers, numbers, keywords, and operators)
• We will also study context-free languages
• Useful for describing the syntax of programming languages.
13

Specifying Language Syntax
• First problem: how to describe language syntax precisely and conveniently 
• Previous last class: described tokens using regular expressions
• Regular expressions easy to implement, efficient (by converting to DFA) 
• Why not use regular expressions (on tokens) to specify programming language syntax? 
14
•
Programming languages need nested, recursive structures, but regular expressions can’t 
handle recursion.
 
 
 
if (x) { y = 1; } else { z = 2; }
This involves:
•
Matching balanced parentheses {} or ().
•
Handling nested if-statements.
•
Matching expressions that can contain subexpressions.
•
Regular languages cannot match:
•
Balanced brackets: { { } { { } } }
require matching opening and closing 
brackets at different nesting levels.

Limitations of Regular Languages 
• A finite automaton that runs long enough must repeat states
• A finite automaton cannot remember # of times it has visited a particular state
• Because a finite automaton has finite memory
– Only enough to store in which state it is
– Cannot count, except up to a finite limit
• Many languages are not regular
• Ex: language of balanced parentheses is not regular: { (i )i | i ≥ 0} 
15
Problem: To recognize this language, the machine must remember (track) number of parentheses 
seen so far: unbounded counting  which finite automata cannot provide.

Contd., Why DFA Is Not Enough
• RE = DFA 
• DFA has only finite number of states; cannot perform unbounded counting 
16
maximum depth: 5 parenthesis 
Why?
•
For every possible depth, the machine would need different information. 
•
Since the DFA has only finitely many states, it cannot support unbounded nesting.

17
The analogy shows the need for a more powerful 
language description mechanism.
Since, Programming-language syntax contains:
•
Nested blocks 
•
Balanced parentheses/brackets 
•
Nested if-else statements 
•
Recursive expressions

The Role of the Parser
• Not all sequences of tokens are programs . . .
• . . . Parser must distinguish between valid and invalid sequences of tokens
• We need
 
– A language for describing valid sequences of tokens
 
– A method for distinguishing valid from invalid sequences of tokens
18

Context-Free Grammars 
• Many programming language constructs have a recursive structure
• A STMT is of the form
 
if COND then STMT else STMT                   , or
 
while COND do STMT                                    , or
 
…
• Here, STMT can itself be another statement, creating recursion
• Context-free grammars are a natural notation for this recursive structure
19

CFGs (Cont.) 
• A CFG consists of
– A set of terminals T
• Actual symbols/tokens that appear in the language. Example: if, +, id, (, ).
– A set of non-terminals N
• Symbols representing syntactic structures.  Examples: S for statement, E for expression.
– A start symbol S (a non-terminal)
• A special non-terminal from which the derivation begins.  Usually represents the complete program or 
sentence.
 
– A set of productions 
• Rules that specify how non-terminals can be replaced.  Example: E→E+E
20

Contd., Let’s begin by defining the parts of a CFG
• A terminal is a discrete symbol that can appear in the language, other wise known as a token from the previous 
chapter. 
• Examples of terminals are keywords, operators, and identifiers. 
• We will use lower-case letters to represent terminals. 
21
•
A non-terminal represents a structure that can occur in a language, but is not a literal symbol. 
•
Example of non-terminals are declarations, statements, and expressions. 
•
We will use upper-case letters to represent non-terminals: P for program, S for statement, E for 
expression, etc. 
•
A sentence → a valid sequence of terminals in a language, while a sentential form is → a valid sequence of 
terminals and non-terminals. 
•
Greek symbols to represent sentential forms. For example, α, β, γ and represent (possibly) mixed 
sequences of terminals and non-terminals. 
•
We will use a sequence like Y1, Y2,… Yn to indicate the individual symbols in a sentential form: Yi may 
be either a terminal or a non-terminal.

Contd., Let’s begin by defining the parts of a CFG
22
• A context-free grammar (CFG) is a list of rules that formally describe the allowable sentences in a 
language. 
• The left-hand side of each rule is always a single non-terminal. 
• The right-hand side of a rule is a sentential form that describes an allowable form of that non-
terminal. 
• For example, the rule A → xXy indicates that the non-terminal A represents a terminal x followed by a non-
terminal X and a terminal y. 
• The right hand side of a rule can be indicate Є that the rule produces nothing. 
• The first rule is special: it is the top-level definition of a program and its non-terminal is known as the start 
symbol.

For example, here is a simple CFG that describes expressions involving addition, 
integers, and identifiers:
1. P →E 
2. E → E+E 
3. E → ident 
4. E → int
23
•
This grammar can be read as follows: 
 
(1) A complete program consists of one expression. 
 
(2) An expression can be any expression plus any ex pression. 
 
(3) An expression can be an identifier. 
 
(4) An expression can be an integer literal. 
•
For shortness: a common left-hand side by combining all of the right hand sides with a logical-or 
symbol, like this: 
 
 
 
E → E + E І ident І int

Notational Conventions & CFG Example 
• In these lecture notes
– Non-terminals are written upper-case. Examples: S, STMT, EXPR
– Terminals are written lower-case. Examples: if, while, id, int
– The start symbol is the left-hand side of the first production
24

Simplified Programming-Language CFG

Examples of CFGs (cont.)
• Grammar for simple arithmetic expressions
25
Meaning of the Productions
•
E → E * E 
•
An expression can be the multiplication of two expressions. 
•
E → E + E 
•
An expression can be the addition of two expressions. 
•
E → (E) 
•
An expression can be enclosed within parentheses. 
•
E → id 
•
An expression can be an identifier.
Important Observation: The grammar is recursive because E appears on both sides of the productions: E→ E + E, E→E∗E
This recursive structure allows the grammar to represent arbitrarily complex expressions.

The Language of a CFG 
• How Does a CFG Generate a Language?
• Productions can be viewed as replacement rules
26
Key Idea
(1) Begin with a string consisting of the start symbol “S”
(2) Replace any non-terminal X in the string by the right-hand side of some production
(3) Repeat (2) until there are no non-terminals in the string 
Suppose: S→aSb, 
                   S→ϵ
Then: S ⇒ aSb, 
               ⇒ aaSbb, 
               ⇒  aabb
Therefore, aabb belongs to the language generated by the CFG.

The Language of a CFG (Contd.,) 
• Let G be a context-free grammar with start symbol S. Then the language of G is:
28
A string belongs to L(G) if:
•
We start from S. 
•
Apply the productions of the grammar. 
•
Continue deriving until no non-terminals remain. 
•
The resulting string contains only terminals. 
Why are they called Terminals?
•
There are no production rules for replacing them. 
•
Once generated, they are permanent. 
•
They represent the actual tokens/symbols of the language.

30
CFGs are powerful because recursive productions allow programming constructs to be nested 
inside one another.
1. Assignment:   id = int
Generated directly using:  STMT → id = int
2. If-else statement
if (id == id) then id = int else id = int
Using: STMT→if COND then STMT else STMT
3. While statement
while (id != id) do id = int
Using: STMT→while COND do STMT
4. Nested while statements
while (id == id) do while (id != id) do id = int
Notice that STMT appears inside another STMT.
5. Nested if statements
if (id != id) then if (id == id) then id = int else id = int

Why do we need parsing?   A compiler needs to:
•
Determine whether the input is syntactically valid. 
•
Determine the structure of the input. 
•
Construct a parse tree or equivalent representation. 
•
Report syntax errors appropriately. 
•
Use a grammar that can be handled efficiently by a parsing algorithm.

Derivations and Parse Trees 
• Note that right-most and left-most derivations have the same parse tree
• The difference is just in the order in which branches are added 
• We are not just interested in whether s ∈ L(G)
 
– We need a parse tree for s
• A derivation defines a parse tree
 
– But one parse tree may have many derivations
• Left-most and right-most derivations are important in parser implementation 
40

Ambiguity 
• Grammar: E → E + E | E * E | ( E ) | int
• String:  int * int + int 
41
This string has two parse trees 
Here * is evaluated first
Here + is evaluated before *
One String + Two Parse Trees = Ambiguity

Ambiguity (Cont.)
• A grammar is ambiguous if it has more than one parse tree for some string
 
– Equivalently, there is more than one right-most or left-most derivation for some string
• Ambiguity is bad
 
– Because the compiler may not know exactly what the programmer intended.
 
 
 
(2+3)∗4=20 whereas: 2+(3∗4)=14
• Ambiguity is common in programming languages
 
– Arithmetic expressions (* has higher precedence than +)
 
– IF-THEN-ELSE 
42
